findings.source_passage: "These things are reciprocal; the ball rebounds, only to bound forward again; for now in laying open the haunts of the whale, the whalemen seem to have indirectly hit upon new clews to that same mystic North-West Passage." —_From_ "_Something_" _unpublished_.
findings.source_locator: near end of Extracts, after McCulloch's Commercial Dictionary
findings.why_it_matters: This self-referential, anonymous 'Something unpublished' citation is critically famous as Melville's probable self-quotation and carries enormous interpretive weight about the book's own ambitions and the mythologization of whaling; it is a recurring touchstone in Melville scholarship.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore verbatim: '"These things are reciprocal; the ball rebounds, only to bound forward again; for now in laying open the haunts of the whale, the whalemen seem to have indirectly hit upon new clews to that same mystic North-West Passage." —From "Something" unpublished.'

findings.source_passage: "In the year 1690 some persons were on a high hill observing the whales spouting and sporting with each other, when one observed: there—pointing to the sea—is a green pasture where our children's grand-children will go for bread." —_Obed Macy's History of Nantucket_.
findings.source_locator: near end of Extracts, after Charles Lamb
findings.why_it_matters: The 'green pasture' image is one of the most quoted lines in the Extracts and carries major interpretive weight establishing Nantucket's mythic status as a seafaring civilization; it is repeatedly cited in criticism on Melville's treatment of Nantucket.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore verbatim as a standalone epigraph entry attributed to Obed Macy's History of Nantucket.

findings.source_passage: "I built a cottage for Susan and myself and made a gateway in the form of a Gothic Arch, by setting up a whale's jaw bones." —_Hawthorne's Twice Told Tales_.
findings.source_locator: after Obed Macy, before Cooper's Pilot
findings.why_it_matters: The Hawthorne citations are among the most critically noted entries in Extracts, signaling Melville's literary friendship and intertextual positioning; their complete absence erases a recognized signature of the chapter.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore both Hawthorne entries (the jaw-bone gateway and the monument for the whale-killed lover) verbatim.

findings.source_passage: "The whale is a mammiferous animal without hind feet." —_Baron Cuvier_.
findings.source_locator: after Paley's Theology, before Colnett's Voyage
findings.why_it_matters: Baron Cuvier's lapidary scientific definition is one of the most quoted single-line entries in Extracts, famous for its deadpan taxonomic register contrasting with the epic quotations surrounding it; its absence removes a key tonal marker.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore verbatim: '"The whale is a mammiferous animal without hind feet." —Baron Cuvier.'

findings.source_passage: "If you should write a fable for little fishes, you would make them speak like great whales." —_Goldsmith to Johnson_.
findings.source_locator: after Goldsmith Nat. Hist., before Cook's Voyages
findings.why_it_matters: This pithy Goldsmith-to-Johnson exchange is widely quoted outside the novel and functions as a witty meta-commentary on the book's own epic register; its absence is a recognizable signature loss.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore verbatim as a standalone entry.

findings.source_passage: "Oh, the rare old Whale, mid storm and gale In his ocean home will be A giant in might, where might is right, And King of the boundless sea." —_Whale Song_.
findings.why_it_matters: The Whale Song is the closing, climactic entry of the Extracts, providing a triumphant tonal cap to the entire epigraph sequence; its absence cuts the structural and rhetorical conclusion of the chapter.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the Whale Song as the final entry to preserve the chapter's closing rhetorical arc.

findings.source_passage: "That sea beast Leviathan..." / Montgomery's World before the Flood long verse passage beginning "In the free element beneath me swam, Floundered and dived..."
findings.source_locator: after Colnett's Voyage, before Charles Lamb
findings.why_it_matters: Montgomery's extended verse catalogue of sea creatures is one of the most evocative poetic entries in Extracts, contributing to the oceanic sublime register that the chapter builds; its absence thins the literary-poetry representation significantly.

findings.source_passage: "And whereas all the other things, whether beast or vessel, that enter into the dreadful gulf of this monster's (whale's) mouth, are immediately lost and swallowed up, the sea-gudgeon retires into it in great security, and there sleeps." —MONTAIGNE.
findings.source_locator: after King Alfred entry, before Rabelais
findings.why_it_matters: Montaigne's entry is tonally distinctive and philosophically resonant, contrasting the whale as terror with the whale as sanctuary; its presence enriches the thematic variety of the Extracts.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the Montaigne entry if word budget allows.

summary: The draft preserves roughly half the source epigraphs but omits multiple high- and medium-weight signatures including the critically famous 'Something unpublished' self-citation, the Obed Macy 'green pasture' passage, both Hawthorne entries, Baron Cuvier's taxonomic one-liner, the Goldsmith-to-Johnson exchange, and the closing Whale Song, constituting signature loss that requires regeneration.
